name: Chapter 5: Morphology of Flowering Plants
description: Root, stem, leaf, inflorescence, flower, fruit, seed, floral formula and Solanaceae

cards.term: Which botanist wrote Plant Anatomy (1954) and Anatomy of Seed Plants (1960)?
cards.definition: Katherine Esau

cards.term: What did Katherine Esau's early work show about the curly top virus?
cards.definition: It spreads through the plant via the phloem (food-conducting tissue)

cards.term: Which five parts characterise all angiosperms?
cards.definition: Roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits

cards.term: Figure 5.1 · Parts of a flowering plant
From what does the primary root develop?
cards.definition: Direct elongation of the radicle

cards.term: What is a tap root system? Example?
cards.definition: The primary root and its branches (secondary, tertiary roots), e.g. mustard

cards.term: What is a fibrous root system? Example?
cards.definition: In monocots the short-lived primary root is replaced by many roots from the base of the stem, e.g. wheat

cards.term: What are adventitious roots? Examples?
cards.definition: Roots arising from parts other than the radicle, e.g. grass, Monstera, banyan

cards.term: Name the three root types in Figure 5.2.
cards.definition: (a) Tap (b) fibrous (c) adventitious

cards.term: Name four functions of the root system.
cards.definition: Absorbing water and minerals, anchorage, storing reserve food, synthesis of plant growth regulators

cards.term: Tap or fibrous: which is typical of dicots and of monocots?
cards.definition: Dicots: tap. Monocots: fibrous.

cards.term: What is the root cap, and what does it do?
cards.definition: A thimble-like structure at the root apex; protects the tender apex as it pushes through soil

cards.term: Describe cells of the region of meristematic activity.
cards.definition: Very small, thin-walled, dense protoplasm; they divide repeatedly

cards.term: Which region is responsible for growth of the root in length?
cards.definition: The region of elongation

cards.term: Where do root hairs arise?
cards.definition: From epidermal cells of the region of maturation

cards.text: From the tip upwards: {{c1::root cap}} → {{c2::meristematic activity}} → {{c3::elongation}} → {{c4::maturation}} (root hairs).
cards.extra: Mnemonic, tip up: Cap, Meristem, Elongation, Maturation: "Can Men Eat Mangoes?"

cards.term: Figure 5.3 · Regions of the root tip
What is the stem?
cards.definition: The ascending part of the axis bearing branches, leaves, flowers and fruits

cards.term: From what does the stem develop?
cards.definition: The plumule of the embryo

cards.term: What are nodes and internodes?
cards.definition: Nodes: regions where leaves are borne. Internodes: portions between two nodes.

cards.term: Name the main functions of the stem.
cards.definition: Spreading out branches with leaves, flowers, fruits; conducting water, minerals and photosynthates

cards.term: What other functions may some stems perform?
cards.definition: Storage of food, support, protection, vegetative propagation

cards.term: How can you tell a stem from a root?
cards.definition: Stems have nodes and internodes, buds, multicellular hairs, and are positively phototropic

cards.term: What is a leaf?
cards.definition: A lateral, generally flattened structure borne on the stem at a node, with a bud in its axil

cards.term: From where do leaves originate, and in what order are they arranged?
cards.definition: From shoot apical meristems, in acropetal order (youngest at the top)

cards.term: What does the axillary bud become?
cards.definition: A branch

cards.term: Name the three main parts of a leaf.
cards.definition: Leaf base, petiole, lamina

cards.term: Figure 5.4 (a) · Parts of a leaf
What are stipules?
cards.definition: Two lateral small leaf-like structures at the leaf base

cards.term: What does the leaf base form in monocots?
cards.definition: A sheath covering the stem partially or wholly

cards.term: What is a pulvinus? Where?
cards.definition: A swollen leaf base, in some leguminous plants

cards.term: How do long, thin, flexible petioles help a leaf?
cards.definition: The blade flutters in wind, cooling the leaf and bringing fresh air to its surface

cards.term: What do veins do?
cards.definition: Give rigidity to the blade and transport water, minerals and food

cards.term: What is venation?
cards.definition: The arrangement of veins and veinlets in the lamina

cards.term: Reticulate vs parallel venation: which is typical of dicots and monocots?
cards.definition: Dicots: reticulate (network). Monocots: parallel.

cards.term: Exceptions worth knowing (beyond NCERT)?
cards.definition: Some monocots have reticulate venation (Smilax, Dioscorea), and some dicots parallel (Calophyllum). Venation is a tendency, not a rule.

cards.term: When is a leaf simple?
cards.definition: Lamina entire, or incisions do not touch the midrib

cards.term: When is a leaf compound?
cards.definition: Incisions reach the midrib, breaking it into leaflets

cards.term: How do you tell a compound leaf from a branch with simple leaves?
cards.definition: A bud is in the axil of the petiole, never in the axil of leaflets

cards.term: Pinnate vs palmate compound leaf? Examples?
cards.definition: Pinnate: leaflets on a common axis, the rachis (neem). Palmate: leaflets at one point, tip of the petiole (silk cotton).

cards.term: What does the rachis represent?
cards.definition: The midrib of the leaf

cards.term: What is phyllotaxy?
cards.definition: The pattern of arrangement of leaves on the stem or branch

cards.term: Name the three types of phyllotaxy in Figure 5.6 with their plants.
cards.definition: Alternate (china rose), opposite (guava), whorled (Alstonia)

cards.text: Alternate phyllotaxy: {{c1::one}} leaf per node (china rose, mustard, sunflower). Opposite: {{c2::a pair}} per node (Calotropis, guava). Whorled: {{c3::more than two}} per node (Alstonia).

cards.term: Why is a flower called a modified shoot?
cards.definition: The shoot apical meristem becomes a floral meristem; internodes do not elongate, and floral appendages form at successive nodes instead of leaves

cards.term: What is an inflorescence?
cards.definition: The arrangement of flowers on the floral axis

cards.term: Racemose inflorescence: axis growth and flower order?
cards.definition: Main axis continues to grow; flowers lateral, in acropetal succession (older below)

cards.term: Cymose inflorescence: axis growth and flower order?
cards.definition: Main axis ends in a flower (limited growth); flowers in basipetal order

cards.term: Trick to remember racemose vs cymose?
cards.definition: Racemose "races on": the tip keeps growing, so the youngest flower is at the top. Cymose "caps" the tip with a flower, so the oldest is at the top.

cards.term: What is the thalamus?
cards.definition: The swollen end of the pedicel (stalk) bearing the floral whorls; also called receptacle

cards.term: Name the four whorls of a flower, outside in.
cards.definition: Calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium

cards.term: Figure 5.10 · Parts of a flower
Which whorls are accessory and which reproductive?
cards.definition: Accessory: calyx, corolla. Reproductive: androecium, gynoecium.

cards.term: What is a perianth? Example?
cards.definition: Calyx and corolla not distinct, e.g. lily

cards.term: Bisexual vs unisexual flower?
cards.definition: Bisexual: both androecium and gynoecium. Unisexual: only stamens or only carpels.

cards.term: What is an actinomorphic flower? Examples?
cards.definition: Divisible into two equal halves in any radial plane (radial symmetry): mustard, datura, chilli

cards.term: What is a zygomorphic flower? Examples?
cards.definition: Divisible into two similar halves in only one vertical plane: pea, gulmohur, bean, Cassia

cards.term: Which flower does NCERT give as asymmetric (irregular)?
cards.definition: Canna

cards.term: What are trimerous, tetramerous and pentamerous flowers?
cards.definition: Floral appendages in multiples of 3, 4, 5

cards.term: What are bracteate and ebracteate flowers?
cards.definition: Bracteate: with bracts (reduced leaves at the base of the pedicel). Ebracteate: without.

cards.term: Hypogynous flower: ovary position? Examples?
cards.definition: Gynoecium highest, others below: ovary superior. Mustard, china rose, brinjal

cards.term: Perigynous flower: ovary position? Examples?
cards.definition: Other parts on the rim of the thalamus at about the same level: ovary half inferior. Plum, rose, peach

cards.term: Epigynous flower: ovary position? Examples?
cards.definition: Thalamus encloses and fuses with the ovary; other parts arise above it: ovary inferior. Guava, cucumber, ray florets of sunflower

cards.term: Figure 5.9 · Position of floral parts on the thalamus
Mnemonic: hypo-, peri-, epi-gynous?
cards.definition: hypo = below (other parts below the ovary), peri = around, epi = upon (other parts on top of the ovary)

cards.term: What are sepals, and what do they usually do?
cards.definition: Members of the calyx; green, leaf-like, protect the flower in bud

cards.text: United sepals: {{c1::gamosepalous}}; free sepals: {{c2::polysepalous}}. United petals: {{c3::gamopetalous}}; free petals: {{c4::polypetalous}}.

cards.term: Why are petals usually brightly coloured?
cards.definition: To attract insects for pollination

cards.term: Name four shapes of corolla.
cards.definition: Tubular, bell-shaped, funnel-shaped, wheel-shaped

cards.term: What is aestivation?
cards.definition: Arrangement of sepals or petals in the floral bud relative to other members of the same whorl

cards.term: Figure 5.11 · Types of aestivation
Valvate aestivation: arrangement and example?
cards.definition: Margins just touch without overlapping: Calotropis

cards.term: Twisted aestivation: arrangement and examples?
cards.definition: Each margin overlaps the next in one direction: china rose, lady's finger, cotton

cards.term: Imbricate aestivation: arrangement and examples?
cards.definition: Margins overlap but in no particular direction: Cassia, gulmohur

cards.text: Vexillary (papilionaceous) aestivation in pea and bean: the largest petal, the {{c1::standard}}, overlaps two lateral {{c2::wings}}, which overlap the two smallest anterior petals, the {{c3::keel}}.

cards.term: What does a stamen consist of?
cards.definition: A filament and an anther

cards.term: How many pollen sacs does a typical anther have?
cards.definition: Bilobed, each lobe with two chambers: four pollen sacs

cards.term: What is a staminode?
cards.definition: A sterile stamen

cards.term: Epipetalous vs epiphyllous stamens? Examples?
cards.definition: Epipetalous: attached to petals (brinjal). Epiphyllous: attached to the perianth (lily).

cards.term: What is a polyandrous condition?
cards.definition: Stamens remain free

cards.text: Stamens united in one bundle: {{c1::monoadelphous}} (china rose); two bundles: {{c2::diadelphous}} (pea); more than two: {{c3::polyadelphous}} (citrus).
cards.extra: Greek adelphos = brother: mono-, di-, poly- "brotherhoods" of stamens.

cards.term: In which flowers do filament lengths vary?
cards.definition: Salvia and mustard

cards.term: What are the three parts of a carpel?
cards.definition: Stigma, style, ovary

cards.term: What is the stigma?
cards.definition: The receptive surface for pollen, usually at the tip of the style

cards.term: To what are ovules attached inside the ovary?
cards.definition: A flattened, cushion-like placenta

cards.term: Apocarpous vs syncarpous? Examples?
cards.definition: Apocarpous: carpels free (lotus, rose). Syncarpous: carpels fused (mustard, tomato).

cards.term: After fertilisation, what do ovules and ovary become?
cards.definition: Ovules → seeds; ovary → fruit

cards.term: What is placentation?
cards.definition: The arrangement of ovules within the ovary

cards.term: Figure 5.12 · Types of placentation
Marginal placentation: description and example?
cards.definition: Placenta a ridge along the ventral suture, ovules in two rows: pea

cards.term: Axile placentation: description and examples?
cards.definition: Placenta axial in a multilocular ovary: china rose, tomato, lemon

cards.term: Parietal placentation: description and examples?
cards.definition: Ovules on the inner wall; one-chambered ovary becomes two-chambered by a false septum: mustard, Argemone

cards.term: Free central placentation: description and examples?
cards.definition: Ovules on a central axis, septa absent: Dianthus, primrose

cards.term: Basal placentation: description and examples?
cards.definition: Placenta at the base, a single ovule: sunflower, marigold

cards.term: Mnemonic for placentation examples?
cards.definition: Marginal: Pea · Axile: Tomato, china rose, lemon · Parietal: Mustard, Argemone · Free central: Dianthus, primrose · Basal: Sunflower, marigold

cards.term: What is a fruit?
cards.definition: A mature or ripened ovary, developed after fertilisation

cards.term: What is a parthenocarpic fruit?
cards.definition: A fruit formed without fertilisation of the ovary (e.g. seedless banana, grapes)

cards.term: What is the pericarp, and its three layers when fleshy?
cards.definition: The fruit wall: outer epicarp, middle mesocarp, inner endocarp

cards.term: What is a drupe? Examples?
cards.definition: Fruit from a monocarpellary superior ovary, one-seeded: mango, coconut

cards.term: Describe the pericarp of mango (a drupe).
cards.definition: Thin epicarp, fleshy edible mesocarp, stony hard endocarp

cards.term: What is special about the mesocarp of coconut?
cards.definition: It is fibrous

cards.term: What is a seed made of?
cards.definition: A seed coat and an embryo (radicle, embryonal axis, one or two cotyledons)

cards.term: Give NCERT examples of one-cotyledon and two-cotyledon seeds.
cards.definition: One: wheat, maize. Two: gram, pea.

cards.term: Name the two layers of the seed coat.
cards.definition: Outer testa, inner tegmen

cards.term: What is the hilum?
cards.definition: A scar on the seed coat where the seed was attached to the fruit

cards.term: What is the micropyle of a seed?
cards.definition: A small pore above the hilum

cards.term: Figure 5.14 · Structure of a dicot seed
Endospermic vs non-endospermous seeds? Examples?
cards.definition: Endospermic: endosperm stores food in the mature seed (castor). Non-endospermous: endosperm used up (bean, gram, pea).

cards.term: Are monocot seeds endospermic?
cards.definition: Generally yes; some, as in orchids, are non-endospermic

cards.term: In maize, how are the seed coat and fruit wall related?
cards.definition: Seed coat is membranous and fused with the fruit wall

cards.term: What is the aleurone layer?
cards.definition: A proteinous layer, the outer covering of the endosperm, separating it from the embryo

cards.term: What is the scutellum?
cards.definition: The single, large, shield-shaped cotyledon of a cereal embryo

cards.text: In maize the plumule is enclosed in the {{c1::coleoptile}} and the radicle in the {{c2::coleorhiza}}.

cards.term: Figure 5.15 · Structure of a monocot seed (maize)
In what order is a flowering plant described?
cards.definition: Habit → vegetative (root, stem, leaves) → floral (inflorescence, flower parts) → floral diagram and floral formula

cards.term: Floral formula symbols: Br, K, C, P, A, G?
cards.definition: Br: bracteate. K: calyx. C: corolla. P: perianth. A: androecium. G: gynoecium.

cards.term: How are superior and inferior ovaries written in a floral formula?
cards.definition: Superior: line below G (G̲). Inferior: line above G (Ḡ).

cards.term: Which symbols show actinomorphic and zygomorphic flowers?
cards.definition: ⊕ actinomorphic; % (or ↑) zygomorphic

cards.term: How are fusion and adhesion shown in a floral formula?
cards.definition: Fusion (cohesion): number in brackets, e.g. C(5). Adhesion: a line drawn above the symbols of the joined whorls.

cards.term: What does the dot at the top of a floral diagram show?
cards.definition: The position of the mother axis

cards.term: Which family does this floral diagram (⊕ ⚥ K<sub>2+2</sub> C<sub>4</sub> A<sub>2+4</sub> G<sub>(2)</sub>) represent?
cards.definition: Brassicaceae (mustard)

cards.term: Read the mustard formula: ⊕ ⚥ K<sub>2+2</sub> C<sub>4</sub> A<sub>2+4</sub> G<sub>(2)</sub>.
cards.definition: Actinomorphic, bisexual; 4 sepals in 2 whorls; 4 free petals; 6 stamens (2 + 4, tetradynamous); ovary of 2 fused carpels, superior

cards.term: What is the common name of Solanaceae?
cards.definition: The 'potato family'

cards.term: Which plant is shown in Figure 5.17?
cards.definition: Solanum nigrum (makoi): flowering twig, flower, L.S., stamens, carpel, floral diagram

cards.term: Solanaceae: habit and stem?
cards.definition: Mostly herbs, shrubs, rarely small trees; stem herbaceous, rarely woody; underground stem in potato (Solanum tuberosum)

cards.term: Solanaceae: leaves?
cards.definition: Alternate, simple (rarely pinnately compound), exstipulate, reticulate venation

cards.term: Solanaceae: calyx and corolla?
cards.definition: Calyx: 5 united, persistent, valvate. Corolla: 5 united, valvate.

cards.term: Solanaceae: androecium?
cards.definition: Five stamens, epipetalous

cards.term: Solanaceae: gynoecium?
cards.definition: Bicarpellary, obliquely placed, syncarpous; ovary superior, bilocular, placenta swollen with many ovules, axile

cards.term: NCERT prints "obligately placed" carpels in Solanaceae. What is meant?
cards.definition: Obliquely placed: the two carpels sit at an angle to the median plane. "Obligately" is a misprint.

cards.term: Solanaceae: fruit and seeds?
cards.definition: Fruit: berry or capsule. Seeds: many, endospermous.

cards.term: Floral formula of Solanaceae?
cards.definition: ⊕ ⚥ K<sub>(5)</sub> C<sub>(5)</sub> A<sub>5</sub> G<sub>(2)</sub>, with a line joining C and A (epipetalous) and the ovary superior

cards.term: Solanaceae: economic importance
cards.definition: Food: Tomato, brinjal, potato; Spice: Chilli; Medicine: Belladonna, ashwagandha; Fumigatory: Tobacco; Ornamental: Petunia
